intro: In this college you'll learn how to look for work in Dutch: describe your personal qualities, use your network, apply for a job, talk about your experience, and shine in a job interview.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — looking for work
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme seventeen. Its title is [[Ik zoek werk]], which means 'I'm looking for work'. Finding a job is one of the most important steps in your new life in the Netherlands, and it asks for a lot of language: you have to describe yourself, talk about what you have done, write a letter, and speak in an interview. Don't worry, we will build it up step by step. First, two key words. A job, the kind you have day to day, is [[een baan]]. The general idea of work is just [[werk]]. So you can say [[Ik zoek werk]], or you can be more specific and say [[Ik zoek een baan in de zorg]], which means 'I'm looking for a job in healthcare'. When a company has an open position, that is [[een vacature]], a vacancy. You might say [[Ik heb een vacature gezien op uw website]], meaning 'I saw a vacancy on your website'. Remember, in this college I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word is spoken by a native voice, so listen closely and repeat out loud. Ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]] Let's begin.

paragraphs.heading: Describing your qualities
paragraphs.text: When you look for work, people want to know what kind of person you are. You describe yourself with adjectives, which are quality words. The pattern is simple: take the verb [[zijn]], meaning 'to be', and add a quality. After [[ik ben]] the adjective stays in its basic form. So you can say [[Ik ben geduldig]], 'I am patient', or [[Ik ben betrouwbaar]], 'I am reliable'. Two of the most useful job words are right there: [[geduldig]] and [[betrouwbaar]]. Put them together and you get a strong sentence: [[Ik ben geduldig en betrouwbaar.]] Other handy qualities are [[flexibel]], which means 'flexible', [[vriendelijk]], 'friendly', and [[zelfstandig]], 'independent'. You can stack a few with the word [[en]], 'and': for example [[Ik ben vriendelijk, flexibel en zelfstandig.]] One small grammar note. When the adjective comes before a noun, you usually add a soft '-e' on the end. So 'a flexible employee' becomes [[een flexibele werknemer]]. A boss might say [[Wij zoeken een betrouwbare medewerker]], 'we are looking for a reliable colleague'. My tip: choose two or three qualities that are really you, and practise saying them with confidence.

paragraphs.heading: Your experience and the perfect tense
paragraphs.text: Now let's talk about what you have done before, your work experience. The word for experience is [[ervaring]]. A very useful pattern is [[ervaring hebben met]], which means 'to have experience with'. For example: [[Ik heb ervaring met klanten]], 'I have experience with customers'. To say how much, use [[veel ervaring]], 'a lot of experience', or [[weinig ervaring]], 'little experience'. To talk about jobs you actually did, Dutch uses a tense called the perfect, and it is essential here. You take a form of [[hebben]], 'to have', and put a special past form of the verb at the very end. The key sentence for you starts with [[Ik heb gewerkt als]], 'I have worked as', and the little word [[als]] means 'as'. So you might say [[Ik heb gewerkt als verkoper]], 'I worked as a salesperson'. Add how long at the front: [[Ik heb drie jaar gewerkt als kok]], 'I worked as a cook for three years'. Notice that [[gewerkt]], the past form of 'to work', jumps to the end of the sentence. That ending position feels strange at first, but it is how Dutch works. Practise: [[Ik heb twee jaar in een winkel gewerkt.]]

paragraphs.heading: Using your network
paragraphs.text: Here is something many newcomers do not know: in the Netherlands, a huge number of jobs are found through people, not through adverts. This is called your network, [[je netwerk]]. So talk to everyone, your neighbours, your classmates, the parents at school, your teacher. A natural thing to say is [[Ik ben op zoek naar werk]], 'I am looking for work', followed by [[Kent u iemand die personeel zoekt?]], which means 'do you know anyone who is hiring?'. You can ask a friend directly: [[Weet jij of er een vacature is?]], 'do you know if there is a vacancy?'. And once you find something this way, you can proudly say [[Via mijn netwerk heb ik deze baan gevonden]], 'I found this job through my network'. A few more useful words: a colleague is [[een collega]], your employer, the boss, is [[de werkgever]], and you, the worker, are [[de werknemer]]. There is also a government organisation that helps people find work and arranges benefits, called the [[UWV]]. If you receive unemployment benefit, they often expect you to apply for jobs actively, so keep a list of where you applied. My warm tip: do not be shy. Most Dutch people are happy to help if you simply ask.

paragraphs.heading: Applying: CV, letter and how to ask
paragraphs.text: Now the real action: applying for a job. The verb is [[solliciteren]], 'to apply'. You can say [[Ik wil graag bij u solliciteren]], 'I would like to apply with you', or be specific: [[Ik wil graag solliciteren op deze baan]], 'I would like to apply for this job'. You will need two documents. The first is your CV, your [[cv]], which lists your education and work history. The second is a cover letter, called [[een sollicitatiebrief]]. You send them together: [[Ik stuur u mijn cv en mijn sollicitatiebrief]]. A Dutch letter has fixed openings and closings, so learn them by heart. You begin with [[Geachte heer of mevrouw]], a formal 'dear sir or madam'. Inside, you mention the advert: [[Ik heb uw vacature gezien]], 'I saw your vacancy'. You close politely with [[Ik hoor graag van u]], 'I look forward to hearing from you', and then the sign-off [[Met vriendelijke groet]], followed by your name. One more set of words: your pay is [[het salaris]], the salary, and a permanent job is [[een vast contract]]. A good question to keep ready is [[Krijg ik een vast contract?]], 'will I get a permanent contract?'.

paragraphs.heading: The job interview — and good luck
paragraphs.text: Finally, the job interview, in Dutch [[het sollicitatiegesprek]]. Let's walk through one in a shop. The manager greets you: [[Goedemiddag, welkom!]] Then she checks why you are there: [[U solliciteert op de baan als verkoper, klopt dat?]], 'you are applying for the salesperson job, is that right?'. You answer warmly: [[Ja, dat klopt. Ik heb de vacature op uw website gezien.]] She asks about experience: [[Heeft u ervaring met dit soort werk?]], 'do you have experience with this kind of work?'. Now your perfect tense shines: [[Ja, ik heb twee jaar gewerkt als verkoper.]] Then the classic question: [[Wat zijn uw sterke punten?]], 'what are your strong points?'. Here you use your qualities: [[Ik ben vriendelijk, geduldig en betrouwbaar.]] She may ask [[Kunt u ook in het weekend werken?]], and you reply [[Ja, ik ben flexibel.]] At the end she says [[Wij bellen u volgende week]], 'we will call you next week', and you close with [[Dank u wel. Ik hoor graag van u.]] That is everything you need. Be yourself, name your qualities, give one small example, and smile. [[Veel succes met solliciteren!]] Good luck — you can do this. See you in theme eighteen!
